claims.text: People have used bamboo since time immemorial to craft utilitarian, decorative and even ritualistic objects, and it features in the craft traditions of many communities.

quotes.quote: used by people since time immemorial to craft a variety of utilitarian, decorative and even ritualistic objects.
In one form or the other, bamboo features dominantly in the craft traditions of many communities.

claims.text: India's bamboo mission describes bamboo as a woody, strong and exceptionally fast-growing grass that is commonly and abundantly available throughout the country.

quotes.quote: woody, valuable, strong and exceptionally fastgrowing grass. It is commonly and abundantly available throughout the country.

claims.text: Rattan's most important product is cane, the stem stripped of its leaf sheaths, which is solid, strong, uniform and highly flexible.

quotes.locator: Species profiles: rattans, 4. The Uses of Rattan
quotes.quote: The most important product of rattan palms is cane; this is the rattan stem stripped of its leaf sheaths. This stem is solid, strong and uniform, yet is highly flexible.

claims.text: Rattans are spiny climbing palms of the subfamily Calamoideae, with around 600 species in 13 genera found only in the Old World tropics.

quotes.locator: Species profiles: rattans, Rattan Taxonomy and Distribution
quotes.quote: Rattans are climbing palms belonging to the Palm family (Palmae or Arecaceae). There are around 600 different species of rattan belonging to 13 genera and these are concentrated solely in the old world tropics;

quotes.quote: Rattans belong to the Calamoideae, a large sub-family of palms.

quotes.locator: Species profiles: rattans, Rattan Taxonomy and Distribution
quotes.quote: all of these climbing palms are spiny, a necessary pre-adaptation to the climbing habit

claims.text: Rattan is one of the most useful forest products in India, a commodity for the furniture and handicraft industries, and many people in remote areas earn their living by extracting and cleaning it.

quotes.locator: Status of rattan resources and uses in South Asia (C. Renuka), 2. India
quotes.quote: Rattans are recognized as one of the most useful forest products in India and the resource plays an important role in the rural economy, employing many people in the remote areas who earn their living through extraction and cleaning of rattans.

claims.text: In North-East India, bamboo craftsmanship is popular and widespread among the ethnic groups, although it is not an exclusive occupation.

quotes.quote: The North-Eastern population comprises a diverse mix of tribes and ethnicities.
The skill of bamboo craftsmanship is quite popular and widespread amongst the ethnic groups, although it is not an exclusive occupation for the people (Shirali 1983).

claims.text: Mongabay India reported in 2024 that bamboo is used extensively by Tripura's tribal and rural communities and that approximately 1.49 lakh artisans there make products from it.

quotes.quote: Bamboo is a prominent non-wood forest resource extensively used by tribal and rural communities in Tripura.
Approximately 1.49 lakh artisans are actively involved in making several products of this unique grass.
Banner image: An artisan showcasing bamboo products in Saras Mela organised in Noida in February 2024.

claims.text: NABARD's Tripura study describes the state as known for its exquisite bamboo and cane crafts, alongside handwoven textiles and terracotta pottery.

quotes.quote: Tripura, known for its exquisite bamboo and cane crafts, handwoven textiles, and terracotta pottery, reflects the artistic legacy of the region

claims.text: Reed baskets and mats are woven across Kerala, with the largest concentration of craftspeople in Angamally, Thiruvananthapuram, Dedunganda, Aryanad and Malapuram, Asia InCH notes.

quotes.quote: This most utilitarian yet critical craft of weaving reed baskets and mats is practiced across Kerala though the largest concentration of craftspeople is in Angamally, Thiruvananthapuram, Dedunganda, Aryanad in Ernakulam district and in Malapuram.

claims.text: In Assam, bamboo baskets come in innumerable types and shapes, each district has its own style, and the men of the household usually weave them.

quotes.quote: There are innumerable types and shapes of the bamboo basket, varying with the use to which they are put. The men of the household usually weave the bamboo baskets. Each district has its own distinctive style.

claims.text: In Chhattisgarh the Bansors, considered a sub-caste of the Birchors, slice bamboo into fine splits called rikas, and whole families practise basketry.

quotes.quote: The Bansors or basketeers are considered to be a sub-caste of the Birchors who slice bamboos into rikas or fine splits and worship the deity Dasha.
Basketry is a craft practised by entire families.

claims.text: Village Square reports that older women of the Muthuvar, Urali, Mannan, Malayar and Kadar communities know how to weave an authentic Kannadippaya, a mat made almost entirely by women.

quotes.quote: Grannies of the Muthuvar, Urali, Mannan, Malayar and Kadar communities know how to weave an authentic Kannadippaya.
The mat is made almost entirely by women.

quotes.quote: Bamboo culms have been used by people and communities for thousands of years, to build houses, fences and bridges.

quotes.quote: Long before plastics were invented, such containers have been fashioned and used.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, however, it was the Parayas and Kaatakaras (literally, forest people) of Anapandan, a hillside near Thrissur who undertook the making of cane and bamboo baskets using plain, twill and occasionally the hexagonal weave.

quotes.quote: 4. Finishing: The crafted items are polished, and sometimes lacquered or stained to enhance their appearance and durability.

quotes.locator: Crafts practiced in Tripura, 1. Handicrafts of bamboo, process
quotes.quote: Bamboo strips are woven or assembled using techniques such as braiding, weaving, and lashing. Tools like knives and pliers are used for shaping and assembly.

claims.text: Felling bamboo in winter, its dormant dry season, gives culms with lower starch and a lower chance of borer attack.

quotes.quote: During the dry season: Winter is the period of dormancy of the bamboo plant. During this period, the plant is acquiring and conserving nutrients for the next season of growth; starch content is lower; and the chances of borer attack, now and later, is lower.

quotes.locator: 05 Selection of Bamboo, Harvesting of Bamboo
quotes.quote: It is best to harvest bamboo in the dry season; harvesting in the rainy season or when the bamboo is flowering should be avoided.

claims.text: A bamboo preservation review says dry-season bamboo is more prone to fungi from increased starch, so the right time to harvest is during or after the rains.

quotes.quote: During the dry seasons, susceptibility to attack by fungi is greater because of the increased starch content. Thus, the right time to harvest is during or after the rainy season.

claims.text: Because harvesting in low-starch periods is not very practicable owing to variability, a Kerala Forest Research Institute study suggests felling in July to November, when amylase activity and starch depletion are relatively higher.

quotes.locator: Post Harvest Protection of Bamboo from Insect Borers (KFRI, Peechi)
quotes.quote: Post Harvest Protection of Bamboo from Insect Borers by a Technique Enhancing Starch Hydrolysis (KFRI, Peechi)

quotes.locator: Post Harvest Protection of Bamboo from Insect Borers (KFRI, Peechi), conclusions
quotes.quote: Since harvesting during the low starch periods is not much practicable due to variability, it will be reasonable to schedule harvesting operation for the period when amylase activity and starch depletion are relatively higher (July-November).

claims.text: Bamboo culms under 3 years old tend to have more starch; in addition their lignification is incomplete, so they are weaker and usually collapse on drying.

quotes.quote: Immature bamboo culms (< 3 years old) tend to have higher starch content. In addition, the process of lignification is not complete, and they will be less strong and usually collapse on drying

claims.text: Felled culms kept upright in a sunny place with their foliage for 3-4 days after felling lose some of their starch.

quotes.quote: At or near the harvest site, keep the culms stacked vertically in a sunny place. with the foliage (leaves, branches) intact. Kept in this way for 3-4 days after felling, the starch content in the culms will be lowered

claims.text: The culm-container manual says cut bamboo stood vertically in a sunny spot with its leaves and branches for 2-3 days keeps photosynthesising, which reduces its starch.

quotes.quote: Post-harvest, the cut bamboo with its leaves and branches intact should be stored vertically in a sunny spot for 2-3 days for the photosynthesis process to continue. This helps to reduce the starch content in the bamboo.

claims.text: Leaching bamboo in water removes starch, keeps it pliable and makes it more permeable to later diffusion and pressure treatment.

quotes.quote: Leaching helps remove starch and also enhances permeability for future treatment by diffusion and pressure.
Storage in water causes leaching of starch and maintains pliability.

claims.text: Villagers preserve fresh bamboo poles by keeping them weighted under stagnant or flowing water for about 3 months, which may ferment or wash out starch and carbohydrates.

quotes.quote: Submerging the bamboo culms in running or stagnant water helps the villagers to preserve the bamboo.

As the culms are lighter than water, weight is put on the culms to submerge them completely in water. The fresh poles are stored for about 3 months in stagnant or flowing water. Starch, carbohydrates, and other water-soluble substances may be fermented or washed out.

claims.text: The culm-container manual says soaking culms in water for a few weeks right after felling leaches starch, giving some protection from borers but not from fungi.

quotes.quote: The bamboo culms can be seasoned by soaking in water for a few week, immediately after felling. The starch in the bamboo leaches out into the water, providing the bamboo some protection from borer attacks. However, this seasoning does not prevent fungus attacks.

claims.text: In field conditions, water-leached bamboo resisted insect and microbial attack for only up to six months, though much better than the control, and was not fully protected.

quotes.quote: the ability of treated samples to resist insect and microbial attack under field conditions only lasted up to six months, which was much better than the control.
The water leaching method was found to be incapable of giving complete protection to the culms under field conditions.

claims.text: In West Bengal, slatted bamboo for paddy-bin matting is seasoned by soaking it in a mud bed for three to four weeks.

quotes.quote: Paddy bins or containers for storing paddy are usually made of bamboo matting.
The bamboo which is used for this is slatted, and seasoned by soaking it in a mud bed for three to four weeks.

claims.text: Smoking culms over the hearth lowers their moisture so that biological degradation cannot take place, and smoke deposits form a protective layer of tar on the culm.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, culms are stored over the hearth or fireplace. The moisture content in smoked culms is thus reduced so that biological degradation cannot take place. Built-up deposits from smoke form a protective layer on the culm.
Smoking reduces moisture content and imparts a protective layer of tar on culm surface.

claims.text: Culms smoked for longer with their own branches and leaves become inedible to insects, the smoking running at air temperatures of 50 to 60 °C.

quotes.quote: If bamboo culms are fumigated (using their own branches and leaves) for a longer time, they become inedible to insects. The culms are smoked at an air temperature of 50 to 60 °C

claims.text: No scientific data on the smoke treatment of bamboo are found in the literature, and the most effective smoking duration is not reported.

quotes.quote: However, no scientific data on the smoke treatment process for bamboo species can be found in the literature.
The most effective duration of smoking for producing high resistance in bamboo is not reported in the literature.

claims.text: Crooked bamboo culms are straightened by baking, rotating them over an open flame to prevent localised heating.

quotes.quote: Baking on open fire has been used to straighten crooked bamboo culms. Bamboo is rotated on an open flame to prevent localised heating.

claims.text: In traditional heat treatment, bamboo is rubbed with castor oil and heated over a gentle fire; a tarry substance oozes out and the bamboo turns dark brown.

quotes.quote: In the process, the bamboo is rubbed with castor oil and then heated over a gentle fire. A tarry substance oozes out of the bamboo and the bamboo becomes dark brown in colour.

claims.text: Traditional bamboo treatments are simple and protect to a degree against borers, but not fully against termites and fungi, and are unsuited to long-term protection.

quotes.quote: The traditional methods are simple and offer protection to a degree against borers. However, these methods do not offer total protection against termites and fungus.
They are simple and cost-effective without the use of supporting equipment. But these methods are not appropriate for long-term protection of bamboo.

claims.text: The culm-container manual has culms immersed for half an hour in a 5 percent solution of borax and boric acid mixed 1:1.5.

quotes.locator: 06 Treatment, Treatment for Whole Bamboo Containers
quotes.quote: Borax and Boric Acid is mixed in the ratio of 1:1.5, which is then used to make a 5 percent solution in water. Now the culms can be immersed in this solution for half an hour.

claims.text: In the modified Boucherie method, a tank two-thirds full of preservative is pumped to 1 to 1.4 kg/cm2, forcing it into the butt end of the culm while the sap drains from the top.

quotes.quote: Modified Boucherie method: In this process, two thirds of a tank is filled with a preservative solution and a hand-pump is used to raise the pressure on the solution to between 1 and 1.4 kg/cm2.
The preservative solution is forced by pressure into the butt end of the trunk whilst the sap drains away from the top end.
In this method, the preservative is forced under pressure through the entire length of the culm, so that the sap is replaced by the preservative.
Bamboos may be treated either by a simple sap displacement technique or by the modified Boucherie process.

quotes.locator: Part two, 2.3.2 Modified Boucherie technique, Procedure
quotes.quote: Fill the tank with preservative solution to about two-thirds full.

quotes.locator: Part two, 2.3.2 Modified Boucherie technique, Procedure
quotes.quote: Develop a pressure of 1.0 to 1.4 Kg/cm2 in the tank

claims.text: In Tripura, cane and bamboo are split vertically into extremely fine, uniform strips with simple tools, keeping the waxy top layer and removing the rougher fibrous inner layer.

quotes.quote: The cane and bamboo handicrafts of Tripura are known for their elegance and exquisite designs.

Cane and bamboo are split vertically and made into extremely fine and uniform strips, using simple tools. The waxy top layer is used while the inner layer, which is fibrous and rougher than the outer layer, is removed.

claims.text: In Odisha the craft begins with splitting bamboo into fine strips that are then woven by hand, a skill passed from older to younger generations.

quotes.quote: The craft process begins with splitting bamboo into fine strips, which are then woven by hand-a skill passed from older to younger generations, often involving both men and women.

claims.text: The skin of bamboo, whose silica tends to repel paints and polishes, is peeled off slowly with a sharp knife before polishing or painting.

quotes.quote: This is a process used to take off the skin of bamboo prior to polishing or painting. The skin contains silica, which tends to repel paints and polishers.
In this process, the skin of bamboo is peeled of slowly with a sharp knife.

claims.text: A rattan processing review notes that villagers soften the part of a rattan stem to be bent with a blowtorch, whose burn marks must later be scraped off.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 7. Secondary Processing
quotes.quote: scraping is required to remove the burn marks of blowtorch, which is used by the villagers to soften the respective portion of a stem for bending.

claims.text: West Bengal cane furniture is made with simple tools such as a hammer, handsaw and dao, by cutting the cane, bending it with heat, fixing it with nails and binding, then sandpapering and varnishing.

quotes.quote: Simple tools such as hammer, handsaw and dao/cutting tool are used to create sturdy cane furniture.
The process of furniture making includes cutting the cane, bending it with heat and attaching with nails and binding. Lastly, sandpapering and varnishing is done to finish the item.

claims.text: A 2002 FAO review reports that air-drying is the most common way to reduce the moisture of rattans in India, and that oil curing methods were recently introduced, citing studies from 1990 and 1992.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), Curing

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), Curing

quotes.locator: Status of rattan resources and uses in South Asia (C. Renuka), 2.3 Processing and preservation techniques
quotes.quote: The standardized curing method uses diesel - coconut oil mixture (9: 1 ratio) or kerosene.

claims.text: Primary processing of rattan includes deglazing to remove the silicified epidermis, fumigation, bleaching, oil curing and drying.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), Major Characteristics
quotes.quote: They include primary processing of deglazing to remove the silicified epidermis, fumigation, bleaching, oil curing and drying.

claims.text: Basketry has two basic techniques, the coiled technique and the plaited or woven technique, with cane a flexible and pliant raw material.

quotes.quote: Cane, the raw material for basketry is flexible and pliant and can be used in a variety of ways. There are two basic techniques used for basketry: the coiled technique and the plaited or woven technique.
The baskets made today are either coiled or plaited and are classified according to their function of carrying or storing.

claims.text: In 2006 the culm-container manual noted that many bamboo craftspersons still used only a single tool, normally a dao or a machete.

quotes.locator: Foreword, signed by the Mission Director
quotes.quote: Mission Director January 2006

claims.text: Tripura bamboo artisans work with the chaku or knife, the broad-bladed takkal, the haath dao bill hook, files and chisels.

quotes.quote: The tools used in making bamboo handicrafts are chaku/knife, takkal/broad-bladed knife, haath dao/bill hook knife, files, and chisels.

claims.text: Baking's high temperatures destroy the starch and other sugars in bamboo, produce tar in its structure and kill any existing infestation.

quotes.quote: The high temperatures destroy the starch and other sugars and also produce tar in the structure. It kills existing infestations if any.

claims.text: Lime washing coats culms and mats with slaked lime, which turns into calcium carbonate that inhibits water absorption and delays fungal attack.

quotes.quote: Culms and mats are painted with slaked lime(Ca(OH) ) which is then transformed 2 into calcium carbonate, CaCO , which inhibits water absorption and 3 delays fungal attack.
Slaked lime makes the surface of treated bamboo alkaline. This delays the attack of fungi.

claims.text: Boron salts, usually boric acid mixed with borax, protect bamboo against borers, termites and fungi except soft rot fungi, and at high concentrations retard fire.

quotes.quote: These are usually a mixture of boric acid:borax. Readymade formulation (disodium octaborate 1:1.4) is also available. Boron salts are effective against borers, termites and fungi (except soft rot fungi). High concentration salts have fire-retardant properties.
Boron salts are effective against termites and fungi. They are not toxic, and when used in concentrated solutions impart a degree of fire retardance as well.

claims.text: Boric acid and borax leach out of treated bamboo, so their use is restricted to bamboo kept dry, under cover and away from rain and ground contact.

quotes.quote: These are leachable solutions and their use is restricted to bamboo used in dry conditions and under cover. Bamboo treated with these preservatives should not be exposed to rain or ground contact.
Common example: Boric acid: Borax & copper sulphate

quotes.locator: Complexes to Reduce Boron Leaching, p. 10616
quotes.quote: Boric acid preservative is associated with the disadvantage of leaching under outdoor conditions.

claims.text: Boric acid dissolves in water only to about 5%, but mixing it with borax markedly increases its solubility.

quotes.locator: Complexes to Reduce Boron Leaching, p. 10616
quotes.quote: The solubility of boric acid in water is about 5%. However, when mixed with borax, the solubility of boric acid markedly

quotes.locator: Complexes to Reduce Boron Leaching, p. 10617
quotes.quote: increases. This is an excellent preservative for protecting wood indoors because it is highly soluble in water.

claims.text: Some Calamus species have a highly silicified epidermis, and when it is removed by deglazing the silica layer snaps off in flakes.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 7. Secondary Processing
quotes.quote: Especially some Calamus species possess a highly silicified epidermis, which is taken off in different ways (deglazing), whereby the silica layer snaps off in flakes.

claims.text: Fumigating canes with sulphur dioxide both sterilizes them and improves their surface quality.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 6. Grading
quotes.quote: Fumigation with sulphur dioxide does not only sterilize the canes, but it also improves surface quality.

claims.text: Bamboo fibres along the cortex contain lignin and silica, which strengthen the culm's outermost layer.

quotes.quote: Bamboo fibres along the cortex contain lignin and silica, which strengthen the outermost layer.

claims.text: The outer skin of bamboo is high in silica, which restricts the flow of preservative into the culm, and its waxy layer is hard to penetrate.

quotes.locator: Need for eco-friendly preservation techniques, p. 10605
quotes.quote: The outer skin of bamboo is high in silica content. This restricts the flow of preservative into the culm. It is also difficult to penetrate inside the waxy layer of bamboo (Janssen 2000).

claims.text: Rattan epidermis is often heavily encrusted with amorphous silica, which hinders processing and is removed; rattan silica content varies among species from 0.9 to 2.7%.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 8.1 Structural properties
quotes.quote: The outer part, the epidermis, is often heavily encrusted with amorphous silica, which hinders processing and is therefore removed. The silica content varies considerably among species (0.9-2.7%).

claims.text: Because bamboo fibres run along the internodes and turn transverse only at the nodes, a culm splits easily along its length once a cut is started.

quotes.quote: Bamboo fibres run longitudinally down the internodal portion, making splitting easier. At the node, the bamboo fibres run transversely.
Due to the fact that the fibres run along the length of the bamboo (except at the node), once the initial cut is made, the bamboo splits easily along its length.

claims.text: The share of fibre, the specific gravity and the strength of bamboo all increase from the inside of the culm wall outwards and from bottom to top.

quotes.quote: the percentage of fibre in the culm wall increases from the inside of the culm wall to the outside, and from the bottom to the top. Consequently, specific gravity and strength properties of bamboo increase from the inside of the culm wall to the outside, and from the bottom to the top.

claims.text: At the nodes bamboo fibres are shorter and turn transverse, giving higher specific gravity, lower shrinkage and lower tensile strength than the internodes.

quotes.quote: Fibres of the bamboo become shorter at the nodes; also, their orientation changes from axial to transverse direction. This results in higher specific gravity, lower volume shrinkage and lower tensile strength compared to the internodes.

claims.text: Bamboo has no radial pathways like the ray cells of wood, so preservative moves sideways between cells only by slow diffusion.

quotes.quote: There are no radial pathways in the culm tissues, like the ray cells in wood, and lateral cell-to-cell movement of preservative depends on a slow diffusion process.

quotes.locator: Need for eco-friendly preservation techniques, p. 10605
quotes.quote: The absence of ray cells in bamboo also constrains the flow of preservative to only the longitudinal direction.

claims.text: Conducting tissues make up only 8% of bamboo culm tissue, against 70% in softwoods, which makes bamboo difficult and slow to treat.

quotes.quote: The extent of conducting tissues are only 8% of the culm tissues, in comparison to 70% for softwoods
making treatment of bamboo a difficult and timeconsuming process.

claims.text: Rattan fibres are 0.9 to 2.9 mm long, averaging 1.3-1.8 mm, and rattan density ranges from 0.3 to 0.6 grams per cubic centimetre.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 8.1 Structural properties
quotes.quote: Fibre length varies between 0.9 and 2.9 mm with an average of 1.3-1.8 mm. Density varies between. 0.3 and 0.6 g/ cm3

claims.text: A typical bamboo culm wall consists of 52% parenchyma cells, 8% conducting vessels and 40% fibres.

quotes.quote: A typical culm wall structure consists of parenchyma cells (52%), conducting vessels (8%) and fibres (40%).

claims.text: The axially oriented parenchyma cells of the culm wall's ground tissue store nutrients, mainly starch and carbohydrates.

quotes.quote: The ground tissues of the culm wall consist of parenchyma cells. These cells are axially oriented. Their large volume provide for storage of nutrients, mainly starch and carbohydrates.

claims.text: Untreated bamboo lasts less than five years; unlike teak it holds no toxic deposits, and its starch makes it more attractive to microorganisms.

quotes.quote: Without any protective treatment its durability is less than five years. Unlike varieties of timber like teak, bamboo structure is void of toxic deposits. The presence of starch makes it more attractive to microorganisms.
It has been found that untreated bamboo has a service life of only two to five years.

quotes.quote: A cross-sectional view of a rattan stem reveals its principal architecture, consisting of two zones - the periphery with epidermis and cortex; and the central cylinder with vascular bundles with fibrous sheaths embedded in thin-walled parenchymatous ground tissue.

claims.text: A commercial cane has evenly distributed vascular bundles and a cross-section of about 20-25 percent fibres, 45 percent conducting cells and 30-35 percent ground parenchyma.

quotes.locator: Challenges and constraints in rattan processing (W. Liese), 8.1 Structural properties

claims.text: The high silica content of bamboo blunts the edges of knives and machetes, which must be kept sharp with sharpening or grinding devices.

quotes.quote: The high silica content in bamboo makes blunt the sharp edges of tools like knives and machetes. Use sharpening or grinding devices to maintain the effectiveness of these tools.

claims.text: Kerala has around 11 kinds of thin-walled reed bamboos of the genus Ochlandra, used mainly by traditional artisans for weaving.

quotes.quote: Kerala has a large number of (around 11) types of thin walled bamboos called reeds (Ochlandra genera) which are used mainly for weaving purposes by the traditional artisans.

claims.text: In Kerala, thick bamboo called mula and thinner bamboo called eeta are made into rough mats used as wall partitions.

quotes.quote: The thick bamboo locally known as mula and the thinner bamboo called eeta are made into rough bamboo mats used as wall partitions and softer grass mats to sleep on.

claims.text: Kannadippaya is woven from the fourth or fifth layer of slivers, which can be made ultra-thin and shiny, split from the reed bamboo Teinostachyum wightii.

quotes.quote: A Kannadippaya is woven with a specific layer of slivers - the fourth or fifth, which can be made ultra-thin and shiny - split out of a reed bamboo species endemic to the region.
Indigenous communities have different names, but it's better known as Teinostachyum wightii (Munro) Bedd among scientists.

claims.text: In Tripura, the extremely strong and solid Bambusa affinis is used as a substitute for cane in furniture making.

quotes.quote: Bambusa affinis is an extremely strong and solid species of bamboo used as a substitute for cane to make furniture in Tripura.

claims.text: In Tripura handicrafts, muli bamboo, Melocanna baccifera, gives its moderately hard middle section to furniture and baskets and its more flexible top to mats and winnowing fans.

quotes.locator: Bamboo species locally available in Tripura
quotes.quote: Melocanna baccifera Muli bamboo is known for its thick walls and strength

quotes.locator: Bamboo species locally available in Tripura
quotes.quote: The middle section is moderately hard used for furniture, baskets, and construction materials due to its durability. While the top section is more flexible, employed in making smaller items like mats and winnowing fans.

claims.text: NABARD's Tripura study names Kanak Kaich bamboo as Bambusa tulda, a flexible, soft-textured bamboo that is easy to work.

quotes.locator: Bamboo species locally available in Tripura
quotes.quote: Kanak Kaich Bamboo Bambusa tulda This bamboo is flexible, with a softer texture, making it easy to work with.

claims.text: The culm-container manual gives kanak kaich as the Tripura name of Thyrsostachys oliveri, which it lists as extremely suitable for culm container craft.

These include Bambusa tulda, Bambusa polymorpha, Dendrocalamus giganteus, dendrocalamus hamilitonii, Teinostachyum dullooa and Thyrsostachys oliveri, making them extremely suitable for culm container craft.

claims.text: In West Bengal, bamboo with long fibres and widely spaced internodes goes to basketry, while solid, thick bamboo with close nodes goes to construction.

quotes.quote: The variety of bamboo used for basketry has long fibres and widely-spaced internodes. When the bamboo is solid and thick and has close nodes it is used for construction.

claims.text: Of the Nath-Yogi bamboo gadgets studied in Sivasagar, 31 were made of Bambusa tulda and 3 of Bambusa balcooa, and cane completed 27 of them.

quotes.quote: In 27 items, cane was used as an associated material to complete the making process.
31 items were made of Bambusa tulda Roxb. and only 3 items were made of Bambus balcooa Roxb.

claims.text: A 2002 FAO review puts India's rattans at about 60 species in four genera: Calamus, Daemonorops, Korthalsia and Plectocomia.

quotes.quote: In India there are about 60 species of rattans under four genera, Calamus, Daemonorops, Korthalsia and Plectocomia.

quotes.quote: FOOD AND AGRICULTURE ORGANIZATION OF THE UNITED NATIONS Rome, 2002

claims.text: Most Indian bamboos are sympodial, clump-forming plants whose culms grow clustered together.

quotes.quote: Most Indian bamboos are clump-forming ('sympodial'), and such stems will tend to be clustered together.
Most of the Indian bamboos have sympodial rhizome.

claims.text: According to Odisha's bamboo agency, a new culm emerges with its full diameter and reaches its full height in 60 to 120 days.

quotes.quote: Unlike trees, bamboo does not acquire more diameter as it grow. The new culm emerges with full diameter and it reaches full height in 60 to 120 days.

claims.text: The culm-container manual says a culm reaches its maximum diameter and height in one spurt, typically 80-110 days after emerging.

quotes.quote: An individual culm attains its maximum diameter and height in a single spurt of growth, typically within a period of between 80-110 days after emergence from the ground.

claims.text: The bamboo preservation manual says a culm turns woody rapidly and elongates to its full height within 3-4 months.

quotes.quote: It turns woody rapidly and elongates to its full height within 3-4 months.

quotes.quote: In India 136 species of bamboos in 36 genera are found to exist.

claims.text: Plaited basketry in Tamil Nadu crosses warp and weft, or two wefts, in chequer, twill, wrapped, intertwined and hexagonal work.

quotes.quote: Plaited basketry in Tamil Nadu is made by crossing the warp and the weft or two wefts. Plaited basketry is of various kinds: chequer work, twill work, wrapped work, intertwined work and hexagonal work.

claims.text: Bamboo nails, thin strong slivers cut from a radial section, join bamboo segments, while iron nails can cause splits and cracks, weaken products and rust.

quotes.quote: They are actually thin, strong slivers of bamboo cut from a radial section, and are used to join and hold in place bamboo segments.
Iron nails can cause splits and cracks that are unsightly, and can weaken the structure of the product. They are also prone to rusting, especially when the product is exposed to water.

claims.text: In Katlamara, Tripura, bamboo furniture is made with a dao, hammer, handsaw, file and chisel, its joints drilled, housed and pinned with bamboo nails and its seats and backs woven from splits.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, Katlamara was known for its bamboo poles used in fishing, pole vaulting and boating but the production of furniture is said to have the potential to alter the economy of bamboo artisans.
The joints are made by drilling, housing and pinning with bamboo nails. The frames are made from the whole bamboo whereas the seat and the back are woven from bamboo splits.
The tools used are dao, hammer, handsaw, file and chisel.

claims.text: The Adi, the largest tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, use cane and bamboo to build suspension bridges, sometimes over 200 metres long, spanning a river from bank to bank.

quotes.quote: Arunachal Pradesh has 16 major tribes of whom the Adi group is the largest in number
The Adis are known to use cane and bamboo to build houses and suspension bridges. The bridges are sometimes over 200 metres in length, spanning a river from bank to bank.
The Adi tribes in Siang district also construct bamboo and cane suspension bridges.

claims.text: In many parts of north Bengal, bamboo containers smoked brown, decorated with poker work and bound with cane are used to store, carry and measure oil and milk.

quotes.quote: Bamboo containers - which are smoked to a brown shade, decorated with poker work, with designs burnt in with a red hot point of a steel tool, bound by strips of cane, and fitted with cane handles - are used to store, carry, and measure oil and milk in many parts of north Bengal.

claims.text: In Meghalaya, where Khasi conical baskets are a common sight, the Khasis are famous for weaving cane mats, stools and baskets, and their cane mat tlieng lasts at least 20-30 years.

quotes.quote: Khasi conical baskets (khoks) are a common sight in Meghalaya.

claims.text: The paikwang, a typical Mizo bamboo basket broad at the rim and tapering to the bottom, carries firewood, cotton and vegetables.

claims.text: The Manipuri chengbon is a basket for storing clothes, with a domed bamboo lid and a square black-and-white checked body on four legs.

quotes.quote: Among the variety of baskets, the chengbon has a domed lid made of bamboo. These have a square body of checks, in black and white, rest on four prominent legs and are used for storing clothes.

claims.text: Naga women carry the khopi, a bamboo basket with a footrest, while a basket without a footrest is called a koshie.

quotes.quote: The khopi is a basket of bamboo and is always carried by the Naga womenfolk irrespective of age. It has a footrest
A basket without a footrest is a koshie.

claims.text: In Assam whole culms store rice beer and water; the culm-container manual says water and food culm containers are especially common in the North East.

quotes.quote: Whole bamboo culms are used as containers for storing home-brewed rice beer, for fetching water, and for carrying drinking water.

The most widespread traditional use of bamboo culm containers if for carrying and storing water and food articles. These are especially common in the North East, but are also used in other parts of the country where good-sized bamboo is easily available.

claims.text: Tripura bamboo mats are woven of fine strips on hand-operated looms with rayon threads, and are flexible only along the warp because the weft is rigid bamboo.

quotes.quote: Fine strips are woven on hand-operated looms and joined with rayon threads in a patterned weave placed close together so that the entire screen takes on the texture and pliability of fabric.
As a rule the bamboo mats are flexible only in the direction of the warp as the weft consists of the rigid bamboo splits.

claims.text: Kannadippaya, a mat woven by tribal people of Kerala's Western Ghats, takes its name from Malayalam kannadi, mirror, and paya, mat, for its optical illusion of squares.

quotes.quote: the lesser-known Kannadippaya mat woven by tribes-folks of the Western Ghats range in Kerala

claims.text: In Kerala, rough kotta baskets with short handles are often reinforced with coir, and neat square vatti baskets of slim bamboo splits serve for shopping and storage.

quotes.quote: Kotta or rough work baskets with short handles are often reinforced with coir; vatti or neatly woven square baskets made with slim bamboo splits are used for shopping, storage as well as a makeshift vessel.

claims.text: For Kerala bamboo mat paintings, artisans weave a mat as the canvas, sketch the drawing, paint it in bright colours and frame it in bamboo reed.

quotes.quote: To start, the artisans create a mat of the appropriate size to serve as the canvas. The drawings are then generated by drawing sketches.
The paintings are done in a variety of sizes and bright colours. The mat paintings are finished by framing them in bamboo reed frames.

claims.text: North-East India holds India's largest stock and diversity of bamboos, and the Western Ghats hold the second largest diversity.

with approximately 66% of the bamboo population concentrated in the North Eastern part of the country

lede.text: Cane and bamboo craft works bamboo, a woody, strong and exceptionally fast-growing grass, and cane, the solid, strong and highly flexible stem of climbing rattan palms.

People have used bamboo since time immemorial to craft utilitarian, decorative and even ritualistic objects, and in North-East India bamboo craftsmanship is popular and widespread among the ethnic groups.
The craft is practised in Assam, Tripura and the North Eastern States, and in Kerala, Odisha, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu.
Starch makes bamboo more attractive to microorganisms and rattan liable to fungi and insects; treatments include water leaching, smoking, boron salts and, for cane, curing in a hot oil bath.

sentences.text: Bamboo culms have been used for thousands of years to build houses, fences and bridges, and whole culm containers were fashioned long before plastics were invented.
Storing bamboo culms over the kitchen fireplace so that smoke prevents insect attack is a village practice thousands of years old.
Many uses of rattan have been known to Indian people since ancient times, and ancient books report its medicinal uses.
The Odisha Bamboo Development Agency says the North Eastern States have practised bamboo craft for centuries as their prime source of income.
In Chhattisgarh, baskets, winnowing fans and mats were first made of fragile leaves and later of much sturdier bamboo.

Many decades ago the whole Sambava community of Kurungalloor Colony in Thiruvananthapuram lived by making products from bamboo reeds, and in 1979 the Kerala State Bamboo Corporation began a community mat weaving centre near the colony.
Asia InCH says the history of Kerala's bamboo reed industry may be traced to the 14th century, when Ibn Batuta recorded bamboo mats used as sails on Chinese ships at Kozhikode.

A cane and bamboo pilot project of the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) and UNDP, started in December 1999 and due to end in December 2002, aimed to give artisans modern technology and design inputs.
NABARD's Tripura study sets out bamboo handicraft making as harvesting and preparation, designing, weaving and assembling, and finishing.

Sources differ on the felling season: winter, the dormant dry season, in the bamboo mission's manual; during or after the rains in a review; July to November in a Kerala Forest Research Institute study; while in Nagaland bamboo is collected between July and October.

Sources also differ on culm age: culms under 3 years are weaker and usually collapse on drying in one manual, culms 3-4 years old are the most widely used in an INBAR manual, and Naga craftspeople use bamboo about a year old because stems more than three years old are too brittle.
Felled culms are left upright in a sunny place with their leaves to lower their starch, for 3-4 days in one manual and 2-3 days in another.
Leaching in water removes starch and keeps bamboo pliable; villagers keep poles under water for about 3 months, while the culm-container manual speaks of a few weeks.
Smoking culms over the hearth lowers their moisture and leaves a protective layer of tar, and baking over an open flame straightens crooked culms.

In Tripura cane and bamboo are split into extremely fine, uniform strips; West Bengal cane furniture makers bend cane with heat; and a rattan processing review notes villagers softening cane with a blowtorch for bending.
Oil curing immerses canes in a hot oil bath that prevents biodeterioration and turns the skin ivory white, and India's standardized method uses a 9:1 mixture of diesel and coconut oil, or kerosene.
The outer skin of bamboo is high in silica, which restricts the flow of preservative into the culm, and fibres along the cortex contain lignin and silica.
Rattan epidermis is often heavily encrusted with amorphous silica, which hinders processing and is removed by deglazing, and the silica content of rattan varies among species from 0.9 to 2.7%.
Lime washing coats culms and mats with slaked lime, which turns into calcium carbonate that inhibits water absorption and delays fungal attack.
Baking's high temperatures destroy the starch and other sugars in bamboo and produce tar in its structure.
Boron salts, usually boric acid mixed with borax, protect bamboo against borers, termites and fungi other than soft rot fungi, but they leach out, so treated bamboo is kept dry and under cover.
Boric acid dissolves in water only to about 5%, and mixing it with borax markedly increases its solubility.
Fumigating canes with sulphur dioxide both sterilizes them and improves their surface quality.
The share of fibre, the specific gravity and the strength of bamboo all increase from the inside of the culm wall outwards and from bottom to top.
At the nodes, bamboo fibres are shorter and turn transverse, giving higher specific gravity and lower tensile strength than the internodes.
Because bamboo fibres run along the internodes, a culm splits easily along its length once a cut is made.
Bamboo has no radial pathways like the ray cells of wood, and conducting tissues make up only 8% of its culm tissue, which makes bamboo difficult and slow to treat.
Rattan fibres are 0.9 to 2.9 mm long, and rattan density ranges from 0.3 to 0.6 grams per cubic centimetre.
A typical bamboo culm wall consists of 52% parenchyma cells, 8% conducting vessels and 40% fibres, and its parenchyma cells store mainly starch and carbohydrates.
Untreated bamboo lasts less than five years; unlike teak it holds no toxic deposits, and its starch makes it more attractive to microorganisms.
A commercial cane has evenly distributed vascular bundles and about 20-25 percent fibres, 45 percent conducting cells and 30-35 percent ground parenchyma.
Kerala has around 11 kinds of thin-walled reed bamboos of the genus Ochlandra, used mainly by traditional artisans for weaving.
In Tripura, the strong and solid Bambusa affinis is used as a substitute for cane in furniture, and muli bamboo, Melocanna baccifera, serves furniture, baskets, mats and winnowing fans.
Sources differ on the Tripura name kanak kaich: NABARD's study gives it as Bambusa tulda, the culm-container manual as Thyrsostachys oliveri.
Rattans are spiny climbing palms of the subfamily Calamoideae, with around 600 species in 13 genera, and a 2002 FAO review puts India's rattans at about 60 species in four genera.
Most Indian bamboos are sympodial, clump-forming plants whose culms grow clustered together.
Sources differ on how long a new culm takes to reach full height: 60 to 120 days, 80-110 days, or 3-4 months.

Sources also differ on how many bamboo species India has: around 125 in 23 genera (Tewari 1992), 130 in 18 genera in the 2006 culm-container manual, or 136 in 36 genera according to Odisha's bamboo agency.
Mongabay India reported 136 bamboo species in India in 2024, 125 of them indigenous and 11 exotic.

Dinoderus brevis, D. minutus and D. ocellaris, called ghoon or shothole borers, do the major damage to felled bamboo in storage and use, and attack it even after it has been made into furniture and mats.
Sources differ on starch: the heavily damaged culms in borer-hit stacks are those with abundant starch, yet one study found that Dinoderus minutus progeny did not correlate with starch content.
In storage yards, about 40% of a bamboo stack may be lost to Dinoderus minutus within 8 to 10 months, according to a 1992 study that Norhisham et al. cite.
A 1983 study cited by Norhisham et al. found borer infestation in storage yards highly unpredictable, apparently related not to season but to the quality of the bamboo.
Fungi grow fastest in bamboo at 40 to 80% moisture, while dry bamboo below 20% moisture does not promote fungal growth.
Rattan's high starch content makes it very liable to fungi and insects, and about 20 percent of harvested canes are estimated to become stained.
The 2002 FAO review reports that the growing popularity of rattan furniture in India led to overexploitation, and that commercial rattan species have been seriously depleted in many regions.
North-East India holds India's largest stock and diversity of bamboos, and the Western Ghats hold the second largest diversity.
Indian rattans grow mainly in the Western Ghats, the sub-Himalayan hills and valleys of eastern and northeastern India, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Reed baskets and mats are woven across Kerala, with the largest concentration of craftspeople in Angamally, Thiruvananthapuram, Dedunganda, Aryanad and Malapuram, Asia InCH notes.
Kerala's basketry is largely made by the Christian communities of Ernakulam and Thrissur, and Irinjalakuda, a town in Thrissur, is the main centre for painted and woven mats.
In Odisha, tribal groups including the Mahali and Lodha and communities from Sundargarh, Keonjhar, Koraput and Rayagada districts make a wide array of bamboo articles.
Tamil Nadu's main centres for cane products are Chennai, North Arcot and Thanjavur districts.
A 2024 study of eight Nath-Yogi villages in Sivasagar district of Assam recorded thirty-four traditional bamboo gadgets.
Plaited basketry in Tamil Nadu crosses warp and weft in chequer, twill, wrapped, intertwined and hexagonal work.
In Assam whole bamboo culms store rice beer and water, and culm containers for water and food are especially common in the North East.
Baskets carry local names: the conical Mizo paikwang, the Manipuri chengbon with its domed lid, the Naga khopi with a footrest, and Kerala's kotta and vatti.
Tripura bamboo mats are woven of fine strips on hand-operated looms with rayon threads.
The Adi of Arunachal Pradesh use cane and bamboo to build suspension bridges, sometimes over 200 metres long.
Bamboo nails, thin strong slivers cut from a radial section, join bamboo segments, while iron nails can cause splits, weaken products and rust.
In Katlamara, Tripura, bamboo furniture joints are drilled, housed and pinned with bamboo nails, and seats and backs are woven from bamboo splits.
The 2002 FAO review reports that Kerala's rattan-based industry depends heavily on cane imported from India's Northeastern Region.
The Kerala State Bamboo Corporation, based at Angamaly, supports weaving artisans around Angamaly and set up common mat weaving centres at Cheranalloor and Chulli in Ernakulam district.
Village Square reports that the Corporation promoted only standardised reed mats for ply-boards, inadvertently eroding indigenous craft skills.

The Tripura Bamboo Mission divides the state's bamboo handicraft sector into five subsectors and says the sector has faced stiff competition from bamboo products of Thailand, China and other South East Asian countries.
In the Sivasagar villages, many families rely on bamboo crafts as a primary occupation alongside agriculture.
Mongabay India reported in 2024 approximately 1.49 lakh bamboo artisans in Tripura and approximately two million traditional artisans whose livelihoods depend on bamboo products.
Boron salts are not toxic, so they are recommended for treating woven bamboo strips, baskets and containers that hold food.
The 2006 culm-container manual calls copper chrome arsenic highly toxic and not suitable for products that touch food.
People applying chemical preservatives to bamboo should wear gloves, face masks, eyeglasses and aprons and wash any chemical off the skin at once.
